Empirical Research Plan  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Instrumental-Variables Difference-in-Differences (2SLS-DiD).

•  The policy raised the minimum school-leaving age from 14→15 in Great Britain (GB) in Sept-1947 and in Northern Ireland (NI) in Sept-1957.  
•  A dummy that equals 1 for birth-cohort × region cells first exposed to the higher leaving age provides a powerful, plausibly exogenous instrument for an extra year of schooling.  
•  Because GB and NI adopt at different times, we difference-out common nationwide cohort effects (time FEs) and permanent regional differences (region FEs); the instrument is therefore the interaction Postc × NIr.  
•  2SLS delivers the Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE): the causal earnings return for individuals who stayed in school only because the law required it.  

This design combines the clarity of a cohort-level RD in birth year with the flexibility of DiD (two regions, two policy dates) and the unbiasedness of IV for measurement-error-free returns-to-schooling estimates.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
YearsSchooling = age_left_full-time_education – 5 (or add 1 if using “highest grade completed” coding).  

Instrument (policy dummy)  
Raisedcr = 1 if, in region r, birth cohort c reached age 14 on/after the effective date of the higher school-leaving age.  
 GB cohorts: born 1 Sep 1933 – 31 Aug 1934 and later.  
 NI cohorts: born 1 Sep 1943 – 31 Aug 1944 and later.  

Control group  
Individuals from the same region who reached age 14 before the reform (pre cohorts) and contemporaneous cohorts in the other region that have not yet been exposed.  

Treatment timing  
t = 0 in the first affected cohort; t < 0 are leads; t > 0 are lags.  
This enables an event-study/lead–lag plot.  

No running variable & cutoff needed; we do not implement an RDD per se but can show RD-style graphs with birth-year on the x-axis.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1 (Relevance): The reform raised average schooling by ≥0.25 years in treated cohorts.  
  Highly plausible—historical tabulations show 40–50 % forced to stay an extra year.

A2 (Exclusion / No direct earnings effect): The law affects adult earnings only through additional schooling, not via simultaneous labour-market reforms.  
  Plausible: no accompanying child-labour or minimum-wage change; timing mismatch across regions helps.

A3 (Parallel cohort trends / Common shocks): In absence of the reform, earnings and schooling trends would have evolved similarly in both regions around each adoption date.  
  Somewhat plausible; we will test with pre-trend and placebo checks.

A4 (Stable composition): No selective migration between GB and NI specifically timed to avoid/benefit from the rule, conditional on birth region.  
  Plausible because rules were based on where one attended school at age 14, not current residence.

A5 (Monotonicity): Nobody left school earlier because the leaving age rose.  
  Institutionally guaranteed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Remedies  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1 Differential war-time cohort shocks (WWII for 1939–45 births).  
 • Include cohort-specific controls; drop 1939–45 cohorts as robustness.  

T2 Region-specific macro shocks (e.g., NI Troubles after 1969).  
 • Add region-specific linear or cubic cohort trends.  
 • Estimate separately on pre-Troubles cohorts.  

T3 Measurement error in self-reported schooling/earnings.  
 • IV already mitigates attenuation in schooling.  
 • Winsorise extreme earnings; re-estimate on hourly or weekly earnings.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline (executable)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# Install/load packages
install.packages(c("data.table","fixest","sandwich","lmtest"))
library(data.table); library(fixest); library(lmtest); library(sandwich)

# 1. Data loading
ghhs <- fread("GHHS_1984_2006.csv")       # micro file

# 2. Variable construction ------------------------------------------------
# Birth cohort (year); region: GB=0, NI=1
ghhs[, cohort := year_birth]
ghhs[, region := ifelse(region_code=="Northern Ireland",1,0)]

# Policy exposure dummy ---------------------------------------------------
# Function to flag if cohort reached age 14 on/after reform date
ghhs[, raised := 0L]
ghhs[region==0 & cohort >= 1934, raised := 1L]   # GB 1947 reform
ghhs[region==1 & cohort >= 1944, raised := 1L]   # NI 1957 reform

# Schooling (years) and log earnings
ghhs[, yrs_school := age_left_ft_edu - 5]        # compulsory start age 5
ghhs[, ln_earn   := log(annual_earnings)]

# Keep analytic sample ----------------------------------------------------
sample <- ghhs[cohort %between% c(1921,1951) & age %between% c(28,64) &
               !is.na(yrs_school) & !is.na(ln_earn)]

# 3. Collapse to cohort×region cells --------------------------------------
cell <- sample[, .(ln_earn = weighted.mean(ln_earn, weight),
                   yrs_school = weighted.mean(yrs_school, weight),
                   raised = mean(raised),
                   N = .N),
               by = .(cohort, region)]

# 4. Main 2SLS with fixest -------------------------------------------------
# First-stage and second-stage in one step; cluster by cohort×region
iv_formula <- ln_earn ~ 1 | yrs_school ~ raised | cohort + region
est <- feols(iv_formula, data = cell, weights = ~N, cluster = ~cohort+region)
summary(est, se = "cluster")

# 5. Robustness: add region-specific cohort trends ------------------------
cell[, cohort_c := cohort - 1940]   # mean-zeroed cohort
est_trend <- feols(ln_earn ~ 1 | yrs_school ~ raised | cohort + region + region:cohort_c,
                   data = cell, weights = ~N, cluster = ~cohort+region)
summary(est_trend, se = "cluster")
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Econometric theory and prior UK evidence suggest a 6–10 % increase in annual earnings per additional year of schooling for compulsory-schooling compliers. Because the reform bound a very low-SES margin, returns might be slightly above the usual Mincer 5–7 %. I expect ≈ 8 % (β ≈ 0.08 in log points).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment  
(1 = clearly satisfied; 0 = questionable)  

C1 Strong first stage (F > 10): 1  
C2 Exclusion restriction credible: 0.7  
C3 Parallel trends / no differential pre-trends: 0.8  
C4 No selective migration or composition changes: 0.8  
C5 Monotonicity (no defiers): 1  

Average score ≈ 0.86 → Design is fairly credible but hinges on exclusion and parallel-trend assumptions, which we will probe extensively.
